reason: The court held that the plaint disclosed one cause of action against all defendants despite several incidents, so there was no misjoinder.
The judgment dealt with proof of the deed and an unraised Notaries Ordinance compliance point, not any notary conviction or credibility rule.
The court required inspection on these facts but expressly preserved the judge's discretion and rejected a blanket duty to inspect in every privilege claim.
The court refused natural-justice relief because the State Land recovery statute provided a specific process for a person claiming wrongful ejectment.
The extracted statement omits the material context that the evidence showed divided possession for over 40 years and deeds executed on that footing.
The statement is only a fact-bound comparison of exhibits P4 and D3 and omits why P4 mattered, namely the statutory duty to declare the truth.
The court referred to Evidence Ordinance sections 32(5), 32(6), and 50, not sections 48 and 50.
The holding concerned a prescribed right of way attaching to a mutually deviated route and not the bare proposition that servitudes can be created by prescription.
The judgment construed section 46 of the Judicature Act, so calling it section 46 of Sri Lankan law is too imprecise to be safe.
The court held that Judicature Act section 47 was confined to prosecutions, so notice to the Attorney-General was unnecessary for the Primary Courts information.
The court did not hold the tautological proposition stated; it held only that section 47(3) transfer procedure is restricted to prosecutions.
The court held that a mortgagor under a usufructuary mortgage retains ownership and is treated as possessing through the mortgagee for partition purposes.
The extracted sentence is a contentless abstraction from a fact-specific finding about succession as Viharadhipathy.
The court held that this oral reconveyance agreement and the pleaded facts were insufficient, but left room for a trust if further facts clearly indicated one.
The statement is not a legal rule from the judgment, which held that Rent Act section 29(2) did not exclude Prevention of Frauds section 2.
The court held that a residential letting for not less than five years must comply with section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance.
The no-conviction result depended on the agreement being invalid for want of notarial execution, which the statement omits.
The court held that a power of attorney is construed strictly and that this general power did not authorize Workmen's Compensation proceedings.
The court referred specifically to the Commissioner of Workmen's Compensation, not to commissioners generally.
The court held that the nine-year-old executant could not execute a power of attorney.
The court held that remedies for encroachment may include removal, purchase, or compensation according to the parties' conduct and circumstances.
The court declined interference because of several trade-mark and balance-of-convenience facts, not as a general bar to reviewing ex parte interim injunctions.
The quote reproduces lower-court reasoning and in any event says the agent was not liable when contracting only as managing agent.
The court construed Prescription Ordinance section 3 to prevent a party from setting up a stranger's title where that person was neither joined nor a predecessor in title.
The court held that the Bank must address three questions under Finance Act section 71 and distinguished reviewable jurisdictional questions from policy discretion.
